items.title: Ask AWS who you are and read a trust policy
items.kills: "A role has its own password or access key."
items.read_only_alternative: This task is read-only. It needs no alternative.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Ask AWS STS which principal signs your commands.
steps.expect: Your account ID and an ARN that names a user, an assumed role or the root user.

steps.text: List the names of the roles in your account.
steps.expect: A list of role names. Some names start with AWSServiceRoleFor.

steps.text: Pick one role name from the list as <ROLE_NAME>. Read its trust policy and look for a password or a key.
steps.expect: A JSON document with Effect, Principal and an Action such as sts:AssumeRole. No password and no key.

items.label: checked against docs, not run in a real account

items.title: Watch an explicit deny beat an allow
items.kills: "If one policy allows an action, the request succeeds."
items.read_only_alternative: This command creates nothing. It simulates the allow policy and the deny policy together: aws iam simulate-custom-policy --policy-input-list '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}' '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Deny","Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}' --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]" Expect s3:GetObject to show explicitDeny and s3:PutObject to show allowed.

steps.text: Create a test role that only Amazon EC2 can assume. The role has no permissions yet.
steps.command: aws iam create-role --role-name saa-iam-t02 --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}' --tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=iam-t02
steps.expect: No output. ROLE_ARN now holds the ARN of the new role.

steps.text: Add an inline policy that allows reading and writing objects in one example bucket.
Ask the policy simulator whether the role can read and write an object. The simulator sends no real request.
Add a second inline policy that denies only the read on the same bucket.

steps.expect: s3:GetObject shows explicitDeny. s3:PutObject still shows allowed.
steps.predict: The role now has an allow and a deny for the read, and only an allow for the write. What does each action show?
steps.explain: AWS [first looks for a Deny statement in every policy that applies](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-deny-checked-first), and [an explicit deny overrides an explicit allow](../facts/iam.md#iam-eval-explicit-deny-overrides-allow). The deny names the read and not the write, so the write stays allowed.

steps.text: Fix it: remove the deny policy. No new allow can fix an explicit deny.
Run the simulation a third time.

verify.expect: An error that says NoSuchEntity: the role no longer exists.

still_costs: Nothing: IAM roles and policies have no charge. Delete the role anyway, so that no unused role stays in the account.
items.label: checked against docs, not run in a real account

items.title: Watch a permissions boundary cap a role
items.kills: "A permissions boundary that allows an action gives the role that action."
items.read_only_alternative: This command creates nothing. It simulates an identity-based policy and a permissions boundary together: aws iam simulate-custom-policy --policy-input-list '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/*"}]}' --permissions-boundary-policy-input-list '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:DeleteObject"],"Resource":"*"}]}' --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject s3:DeleteObject --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::saa-example-bucket/report.csv --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]" Expect s3:GetObject to show allowed, because both policies allow it. Expect s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject to show implicitDeny, because each of them is in one policy and not in the other.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Create a test role for a workload on Amazon EC2. Its trust policy names Amazon EC2, and the role has no permissions policy yet.
steps.command: aws iam create-role --role-name saa-iam-t03 --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}' --tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=iam-t03
steps.expect: No output. ROLE_ARN now holds the ARN of the new role.

steps.text: Set the AWS managed policy AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess as the permissions boundary of the role. This policy allows read-only access to Amazon S3.
Read the permissions boundary of the role.
Ask the policy simulator whether the role can read an object in an example bucket. The simulator sends no real request.
steps.predict: The boundary allows reads in Amazon S3. The role has no permissions policy. Does the simulator allow s3:GetObject?
steps.explain: A permissions boundary [does not provide permissions on its own](../facts/iam.md#iam-boundary-limits-but-never-grants). The role can do only what is [allowed by both its identity-based policies and its permissions boundaries](../facts/iam.md#iam-permissions-boundary-sets-maximum-does-not-grant). The role has no identity-based policy yet, so nothing allows the read.

steps.text: Fix it: add an inline policy that allows every Amazon S3 action on the example bucket. This policy allows more than the boundary does.
Simulate a read and a write on the same object. Before you run it, predict which of the two actions is allowed.
steps.expect: s3:GetObject shows allowed. s3:PutObject still shows implicitDeny, although the inline policy allows every Amazon S3 action.

cleanup.text: Remove the permissions boundary from the role.

verify.expect: An error that says NoSuchEntity: the role no longer exists.

still_costs: Nothing: IAM roles and policies have no charge. Delete the role anyway, so that no unused role stays in the account.
